items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable capabilities across diverse tasks, yet their internal decision-making processes remain largely opaque. Mechanistic interpretability-the systematic study of how neural networks implement algorithms through their learned representations and computational structures-has emerged as a critical research direction for understanding and aligning these models. This paper surveys recent progress in mechanistic interpretability techniques applied to LLM alignment, examining methods ranging from circuit discovery to feature visualization, activation steering, and causal intervention. We analyze how interpretability insights have informed alignment strategies including reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), constitutional AI, and scalable oversight. Key challenges are identified, including the superposition hypothesis, polysemanticity of neurons, and the difficulty of interpreting emergent behaviors in large-scale models. We propose future research directions focusing on automated interpretability, cross-model generalization of circuits, and the development of interpretability-driven alignment techniques that can scale to frontier models.</jats:p>
title: Mechanistic Interpretability for Large Language Model Alignment: Progress, Challenges, and Future Directions

items.abstract: <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable performance, prompting the development of LLM-based agents to tackle complex, open-world tasks. Despite these advances, autonomous agents still face critical bottlenecks in environmental perception, multi-step reasoning, and long-term opera-tional consistency. Graphs provide a systematic solution to these challenges by explicitly modeling entities, relationships, and dependencies, thereby establishing a rigorous foundation for reasoning and interaction. While recent literature explores this integration, existing surveys primarily focus on operational workflows and architectures, lacking a systematic analysis of how graphs fundamentally elevate agent intelligence. To bridge this gap, this survey presents a comprehensive review of Graph-Augmented LLM-based Agents (GLAs). We systematically decompose agent architecture to distill five core capabilities required for advanced intelligence: perception, reasoning, memorization, generaliza-tion, and interaction. We explicitly address why graphs are uniquely suited to bolster these capabilities and how they are practically integrated, proposing a novel taxonomy that organizes existing studies along these five dimensions. Furthermore, we review representative real-world applications of GLAs across diverse domains and outline key challenges and promising directions for future research. A curated repository containing the literature reviewed in this survey, along with the latest advancements in this field, is maintained and regularly updated at https://github.com/sqs17/GLA.</jats:p>
title: Augmenting the Intelligence of Large Language Model-Based Agents with Graphs: A Survey

items.abstract: <jats:p>Access Control Management (ACM) is a fundamental security measure of information systems, governing which resources a user can access and under what conditions. Typically, effective ACM requires significant manual effort for policy specification, enforcement, and maintenance. To alleviate this burden, prior research has explored automating ACM by integrating machine learning solutions. However, the emergence of Large Language Models (LLMs) and, more recently, LLM agents has opened up many new challenges and opportunities for information systems. Although a plethora of studies currently focus on LLM security, they primarily address adversarial threats, leaving the specific implications for ACM largely underexplored. In this article, we address this gap by surveying the synergistic integration of ACM and LLM agents from a twofold perspective: agents for ACM, where agents assist security administrators in automating the management of access control; and ACM for agents, where access control principles are applied to regulate the behavior, permissions, and security boundaries of the agents themselves. Through these two lenses, we disentangle and define three core ACM tasks, which are receiving increasing attention but are not yet clearly defined in the literature: access control policy generation, decision-making, and enforcement. Furthermore, we conceptualize agents as three core components of standard access-control models: agents as Subjects, Objects, and Actions. To survey existing solutions, we formalize the interaction flow between users and agents and categorize four restriction mechanisms for ACM: user authentication, agent customization, LLM customization, and tools. Building on these mechanisms, we provide a critical analysis of the state-of-the-art, and finally outline open challenges and future research directions to foster stronger cohesion between ACM and LLM agents.</jats:p>
title: The Synergistic Integration of Access Control Management and Large Language Model Agents: A Survey

items.abstract: <jats:p>The evolution of large language models (LLMs) from passive text generators to autonomous agents capable of invoking external tools, accessing databases, executing code, and interacting with digital environments has significantly expanded their practical utility across diverse domains. While tool-calling architectures enhance problem-solving capabilities and enable dynamic decision-making, they also introduce complex governance and accountability challenges that extend beyond traditional concerns associated with standalone LLMs. Autonomous agents can perform multi-step actions with limited human intervention, creating new risks related to transparency, responsibility attribution, security vulnerabilities, privacy violations, and unintended consequences. This paper critically examines the governance implications of tool-calling LLM agents, focusing on the tension between increased autonomy and the need for effective oversight. The study explores key accountability issues, including decision traceability, auditability, explainability, human-in-the-loop control, regulatory compliance, and liability allocation among developers, deployers, and end users. Furthermore, it analyzes emerging governance frameworks and technical safeguards designed to ensure trustworthy agent behavior in high-stakes environments such as healthcare, finance, cybersecurity, and public administration. The paper argues that existing governance mechanisms developed for conventional AI systems are insufficient to address the operational complexity of autonomous tool-using agents. A multidimensional governance approach integrating technical controls, organizational policies, ethical principles, and regulatory standards is therefore proposed. The findings contribute to ongoing discussions on responsible AI deployment by highlighting pathways for balancing innovation, autonomy, and accountability in next-generation intelligent systems.</jats:p>
title: From Retrieval to Autonomy: Governance and Accountability Challenges in Tool-Calling Large Language Model Agents

items.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of large language models (LLMs) with domain-specific computational tools offers a promising pathway to streamline and enhance materials science workflows. This paper presents MatSciAgent, a multi-agent framework capable of performing key tasks such as materials data retrieval, continuum simulation, crystal structure generation, and molecular dynamics simulation. At the core of the framework is the master agent, which interprets the user’s natural language query, identifies the task type, and delegates it to a corresponding task-specific agent equipped with appropriate computational tools. Leveraging databases such as the Materials Project and MatWeb, the framework retrieves and summarizes materials data with grounded, factual responses—addressing a key limitation of vanilla LLMs. In cases where the target material is not found in existing databases, a generative task-specific agent can propose plausible crystal structures. For simulation tasks, dedicated agents extract relevant parameters from the user query to conduct continuum simulations (e.g., Cellular Automata and Monte Carlo Annealing) and atomistic simulations (e.g., Molecular Dynamics) using both established software and custom code. The modular design of these agents and their associated tools enables seamless extensibility, allowing the framework to evolve as new capabilities are integrated.</jats:p>
title: Modular Large Language Model Agents for Multi-Task Computational Materials Science
